name: formats
description: Every registered format with its metadata, and the site export's measured row (pooled over every cell the format ran in; percent). Rows outside the core eight rest on the export, not on the paper's tables.

go_signature.name: Go function signatures
go_signature.description: Idiomatic Go: exported funcs with `// Name does ...` doc comments and explicit return types.

rust_signature.name: Rust function signatures with serde structs
rust_signature.description: Rust `pub fn` declarations with `///` doc comments and Option<T> for optional arguments — types carry optionality instead of a separate flag.

java_signature.name: Java interface methods with Javadoc
java_signature.description: Java method declarations inside an interface, documented with Javadoc tags. The most ceremonious presentation in the study.

kotlin_signature.name: Kotlin function signatures
kotlin_signature.description: Kotlin `fun` declarations with nullable types for optional arguments and KDoc comments.

swift_signature.name: Swift function signatures
swift_signature.description: Swift `func` declarations with labelled arguments — argument labels give the model an extra naming cue that most languages lack.

csharp_signature.name: C# method signatures with XML doc
csharp_signature.description: C# methods documented with `<summary>`/`<param>` XML comments — a doc style that is itself markup.

c_header.name: C header declarations
c_header.description: Plain C prototypes with block comments. Cannot express optionality or enums natively, so it is our lower bound on type expressiveness.

cpp_signature.name: C++ declarations with std types
cpp_signature.description: C++ prototypes using std::optional and std::variant, so optionality and unions are in the type rather than in prose.

haskell_curried.name: Haskell curried signatures
haskell_curried.description: `toolName :: ArgType1 -> ArgType2 -> IO Result` with named-argument hints only in comments. Tests whether models can bind arguments positionally when the interface gives no keyword slots.

ocaml_signature.name: OCaml val declarations
ocaml_signature.description: OCaml `val` declarations with labelled arguments (~name:type), which keeps names while staying in ML syntax.

scala_signature.name: Scala method signatures
scala_signature.description: Scala `def` declarations with Option[T] and default values.

elixir_signature.name: Elixir @spec declarations
elixir_signature.description: Elixir specs with @doc strings — documentation is a first-class language construct here rather than a comment.

julia_signature.name: Julia function signatures
julia_signature.description: Julia declarations with keyword arguments after a semicolon, which maps cleanly onto required/optional.

ruby_signature.name: Ruby method signatures (RBS-style types)
ruby_signature.description: Ruby `def` lines with an RBS type comment above them.

php_signature.name: PHP function signatures with PHPDoc
php_signature.description: PHP declarations with PHPDoc @param annotations carrying the real types.

lua_signature.name: Lua function declarations with LDoc
lua_signature.description: Lua functions annotated with LDoc `---@param` lines. Everything is a table, so structure lives entirely in the annotations.

zig_signature.name: Zig function declarations
zig_signature.description: Zig `pub fn` with optional pointers (`?T`) and error unions.

r_signature.name: R function signatures with roxygen
r_signature.description: R functions documented with roxygen2 `#' @param` blocks.

matlab_signature.name: MATLAB function signatures
matlab_signature.description: MATLAB `function out = name(args)` with an `arguments` validation block — an unusual but real way to declare types and defaults.

sql_udf.name: SQL user-defined function declarations
sql_udf.description: `CREATE FUNCTION name(arg TYPE DEFAULT x) RETURNS ...` with COMMENT ON statements for the prose. Tools as database functions.

bash_function.name: Bash function stubs with usage comments
bash_function.description: Shell functions with a usage line and `local` variable assignments. Everything is a string here, which makes it the weakest type channel of any code format.

toml.name: TOML tool tables
toml.description: `[[tool]]` array-of-tables with `[tool.params.name]` subtables. Section headers make the tool boundary very explicit.

ini.name: INI sections
ini.description: `[tool_name]` sections with `param = type (required)` lines. About as flat as a structured format can get.

hcl.name: HCL (Terraform-style) blocks
hcl.description: `tool "name" { variable "x" { type = string ... } }`. HCL blocks look like code but behave like config.

cue.name: CUE definitions
cue.description: CUE `#Tool` definitions where constraints are part of the type lattice (`int & >=0 & <=100`). Constraints and types are the same thing here, unlike everywhere else in the study.

dhall.name: Dhall record types
dhall.description: Dhall record types with `Optional` fields. A total, typed config language that almost never appears in pretraining corpora.

jsonnet.name: Jsonnet function definitions
jsonnet.description: Jsonnet `local` functions with default arguments — a config language whose unit of reuse is literally a function.

nix_expr.name: Nix expressions (novel)
nix_expr.description: Tools as Nix functions with attribute-set arguments and `mkOption` style type declarations. Lazily-evaluated config as an interface.

kdl.name: KDL document language (novel)
kdl.description: KDL nodes: `tool "name" { param "x" type=string required=#true }`. A recent, very compact document language most models have barely seen.

edn.name: EDN (Clojure data notation)
edn.description: EDN maps with keyword keys and clojure.spec-style predicates. Data-as-code in a Lisp dialect.

sexpr.name: S-expressions
sexpr.description: `(deftool name (param type required) ...)` — parenthesised prefix notation. Minimal syntax, maximal nesting.

starlark.name: Starlark rule definitions
starlark.description: Bazel-flavoured Starlark rules with `attr.string(mandatory=True)` declarations. Python-shaped syntax, config semantics.

ebnf_grammar.name: EBNF grammar of legal calls (novel)
ebnf_grammar.description: An EBNF grammar whose language is exactly the set of well-formed calls. Optionality is `[...]`, enums are alternations, nesting is recursion. The schema becomes a production system.

gbnf_grammar.name: GBNF constrained-decoding grammar (novel framing)
gbnf_grammar.description: The llama.cpp GBNF dialect used for constrained decoding, shown to the model as the interface rather than enforced at sampling time. Same artefact, different channel.
gbnf_grammar.real_world_origin: llama.cpp GBNF (normally used for decoding, not prompting)

regex_spec.name: Regular expressions over call strings (novel)
regex_spec.description: One regex per tool matching every legal call string. Fully precise for flat tools, awkward for nested ones — which is exactly the trade-off we want measured.

typed_lambda.name: Typed lambda-calculus arrows (novel)
typed_lambda.description: `get_weather : City × Unit? → Weather` in mathematical notation with product and sum types. The most abstract presentation in the study; nothing about it is code-like.

symbolic_compressed.name: Symbolic ultra-compressed notation (novel)
symbolic_compressed.description: A purpose-built shorthand: `weather!city:s?unit:{C,F}` where `!` starts required arguments, `?` starts optional ones, and types are single letters. Roughly the smallest faithful encoding we could design; it exists to anchor the low end of the token-cost axis.

protobuf.name: Protocol Buffers service definition
protobuf.description: A `service` with one rpc per tool and a request message per tool. Field numbers, `optional`, and nested messages carry the whole schema.

graphql_sdl.name: GraphQL schema (SDL)
graphql_sdl.description: Each tool as a Mutation field with typed arguments, `!` for required, enums as real GraphQL enums, and triple-quoted descriptions.

thrift_idl.name: Apache Thrift IDL
thrift_idl.description: Thrift service methods with numbered, explicitly required/optional arguments — the most explicit optionality marking of any format.

avro_schema.name: Apache Avro record schemas
avro_schema.description: One Avro record per tool, JSON-encoded, with union types for nullable fields. JSON syntax but a very different vocabulary from JSON Schema.

wit_idl.name: WebAssembly Component Model WIT
wit_idl.description: WIT interface declarations with option<T>, list<T>, record and variant. A modern, terse IDL that models have seen very little of — a natural test of format familiarity.

smithy_idl.name: Smithy IDL
smithy_idl.description: AWS Smithy operations with `@required`, `@documentation` and structure shapes. Trait-annotated rather than syntax-annotated.

capnproto_idl.name: Cap'n Proto schema
capnproto_idl.description: Cap'n Proto interfaces with numbered fields and inline parameter lists on each method.

flatbuffers_idl.name: FlatBuffers schema
flatbuffers_idl.description: FlatBuffers tables and enums, one table per tool request.

json_schema_openai.name: JSON Schema (OpenAI function shape)
json_schema_openai.description: OpenAI-style function definitions: a list of {"type":"function","function":{...}} objects with a JSON Schema parameters block. The industry default.
json_schema_openai.real_world_origin: OpenAI Chat Completions / Responses function calling

json_schema_flat.name: JSON Schema (flat function objects)
json_schema_flat.description: The same JSON Schema without the outer type/function wrapper: {"name":..,"description":..,"parameters":{..}}. Isolates the cost of the wrapper itself.

json_schema_anthropic.name: JSON Schema (Anthropic input_schema shape)
json_schema_anthropic.description: Anthropic-style tool definitions using `input_schema` instead of `parameters`. Same content, different key.

json_schema_draft2020.name: JSON Schema 2020-12 (full, with $schema and $defs)
json_schema_draft2020.description: Formal JSON Schema 2020-12 documents, one per tool, with $schema, $id and $defs for repeated sub-objects. The most verbose, most standards-correct end of the JSON axis.

json_compact.name: JSON Schema (minified, no whitespace)
json_compact.description: Byte-identical content to json_schema_openai with all optional whitespace removed. Pure token-cost lever with content held fixed.

json_minimal.name: JSON (names and types only)
json_minimal.description: Names, parameter names, types and required flags. No descriptions, no constraints, no returns. Tests how much of a schema's value is the prose rather than the structure.
json_minimal.real_world_origin: Context-budget stripped schemas seen in MCP proxies

names_only.name: Tool names only
names_only.description: A bare list of the tool names, one per line: no parameters, no types, no descriptions. The floor of the schema-component ladder.
names_only.real_world_origin: A tool menu with no documentation

names_then_schema.name: Names, then the chosen tool's schema
names_then_schema.description: Two calls: pick a tool from a bare list of names, then write the call from that one tool's full JSON Schema. The progressive-disclosure policy.
names_then_schema.real_world_origin: A tool menu with lazy documentation loading

names_then_schema_v2.name: Names, then the chosen tool's schema (v2)
names_then_schema_v2.description: Two calls: pick a tool from a bare list of names, then write the call from that one tool's full JSON Schema. No fallback when no tool is named; graded on the original catalogue; both calls' tokens recorded.
names_then_schema_v2.real_world_origin: A tool menu with lazy documentation loading

names_desc_then_schema.name: Names and one-line descriptions, then the chosen tool's schema
names_desc_then_schema.description: Two calls: pick a tool from a list of names with one-line descriptions, then write the call from that tool's full JSON Schema.
names_desc_then_schema.real_world_origin: A documented tool menu with lazy schema loading

oracle_then_schema.name: Oracle selection, then the gold tool's schema
oracle_then_schema.description: One call: the gold tool's full JSON Schema shown alone, as if a perfect selector had picked it. The ceiling of progressive disclosure.
oracle_then_schema.real_world_origin: An upper bound, not a deployment

json_names_params.name: JSON (tool and parameter names only)
json_names_params.description: {"name": ..., "params": [param names]} per tool: which arguments exist, but not their types, structure, requiredness or meaning.

jsonl.name: JSON Lines (one tool per line)
jsonl.description: One complete JSON tool object per line, no enclosing array. Line-oriented layout that many models see during pretraining.

json5.name: JSON5 (unquoted keys, comments, trailing commas)
json5.description: JSON5 relaxes JSON: bare keys, single quotes, and // comments carrying the descriptions. Cheaper in tokens than strict JSON.

hjson.name: Hjson (quote-free human JSON)
hjson.description: Hjson drops quotes and commas entirely. Reads like an indented key/value block while remaining a JSON superset.

jsonc.name: JSON with comments (JSONC)
jsonc.description: Strict JSON structure with every description moved out of the data and into a // comment above its key. Separates prose from structure without removing either.

json_dotted_paths.name: Flattened dotted-path JSON (novel)
json_dotted_paths.description: Every leaf of every schema written as one flat dotted path with its type: `book_flight.passenger.name: string!`. Nesting is encoded in the key, so structure survives with no braces at all.

xml_schema.name: XML tool descriptions
xml_schema.description: `<tool><name/><description/><parameters/></tool>` blocks. The shape several vendors have used for prompt-level tool listings.
xml_schema.real_world_origin: Anthropic legacy tool_description blocks; many agent prompts

xml_attributes.name: XML with attribute-only parameters
xml_attributes.description: Everything moved into attributes so each parameter is one line. Same information as xml_schema at roughly half the tokens.

xsd.name: XML Schema Definition (XSD)
xsd.description: Formal XSD with complexType, xs:element minOccurs/maxOccurs and xs:restriction enumerations. The most verbose format in the study.

html_forms.name: HTML forms (novel)
html_forms.description: Each tool as an HTML `<form>`: inputs with type, required, min/max, `<select><option>` for enums, `<label>` for descriptions. Web forms are exactly a typed argument interface, and models have seen billions of them.

markdown_docs.name: Markdown API documentation
markdown_docs.description: Human API docs: `## tool_name`, a prose paragraph, a bulleted parameter list with types, and a usage example. What a developer would actually read.

rest_endpoints.name: REST endpoint listing
rest_endpoints.description: `POST /tool_name` with a documented JSON body. Frames tools as HTTP endpoints rather than functions.

curl_examples.name: curl invocation examples (novel)
curl_examples.description: Every tool shown only as a runnable `curl` command with a filled example body. There is no abstract schema at all — the model has to generalise from a concrete instance.

contrastive.name: Contrastive schema with disambiguation (novel)
contrastive.description: Standard compact schemas plus an explicit 'not to be confused with' note pointing at the most similar other tool. Tests whether tool-count decay is confusion between neighbours rather than context dilution.

decision_tree.name: Routing decision tree (novel)
decision_tree.description: A nested decision tree over domains and intents that ends in a tool and its arguments. Turns tool selection from a flat search over N options into a shallow traversal.

namespaced.name: Namespaced grouping (novel)
namespaced.description: Tools grouped under a domain namespace with the shared prefix factored out: `calendar { create(...) find(...) }`. Shrinks both tokens and the apparent number of choices at each level.

diff_schema.name: Delta-encoded schemas (novel)
diff_schema.description: The first tool of each domain is written in full; the rest are written as a diff against it (+added, -removed, ~changed). Large universes with shared structure compress hard, at the cost of forcing the model to reconstruct the full schema itself.

slot_template.name: Fill-in-the-blank call template (novel)
slot_template.description: Each tool shown as the literal JSON the model should emit, with typed placeholders in the value slots. The model copies and fills rather than constructs, which should cut schema violations.

state_graph.name: Precondition/effect state graph (novel)
state_graph.description: Tools as edges in a state graph: what must already be known before a call, and what the call makes known. Written for chained tasks, where a signature list says nothing about ordering.

negative_space.name: Schema plus explicit non-uses (novel)
negative_space.description: A compact schema followed by 'do not use this when ...' lines derived from the sibling tools. Aimed at the null-case and wrong-tool failure modes rather than at argument accuracy.

progressive.name: Progressive disclosure, three layers (novel)
progressive.description: Layer 1 is a one-line index of every tool. Layer 2 gives argument names only. Layer 3 gives full types and docs. All three are in context at once, cheapest first, so the model can stop reading as soon as it is sure.

worked_dialogue.name: Worked mini-transcripts (novel)
worked_dialogue.description: For each tool, a two-line transcript: a plausible user request and the exact call that answers it. No abstract schema — the interface is entirely demonstration, in the same shape as the task the model is about to be given.

question_slots.name: Arguments as questions (novel)
question_slots.description: Each argument written as the question the tool is asking: 'Which city? (text, required)'. Reframes argument binding as answering rather than as filling a structure.

type_indexed.name: Indexed by argument type (novel)
type_indexed.description: Inverts the listing: group by argument name and type, then say which tools use each. Answers 'I have a city and a date, what can I call?' directly.

emoji_semantic.name: Symbol-channel notation (novel)
emoji_semantic.description: Types encoded as single symbols outside the Latin alphabet, so type information costs one token and never collides with an English word. A deliberate stress test of whether type signals have to be linguistic at all.

checklist.name: Schema with pre-call checklist (novel)
checklist.description: A normal compact schema followed by a short checklist the model is told to run before emitting a call (every required field present, enums from the listed set, no invented fields). Targets schema-violation rate directly rather than tool choice.

capability_matrix.name: Tool × argument matrix (novel)
capability_matrix.description: A single matrix: rows are tools, columns are the union of all argument names, cells mark required/optional/absent. The whole universe becomes one object the model can scan in either direction.

natural_language.name: Natural-language tool descriptions
natural_language.description: A short paragraph per tool: what it does, what it needs, and what is optional — written as prose with no schema syntax anywhere.
natural_language.real_world_origin: Natural Language Tools (NLT) line of work

nl_terse.name: One-sentence tool summaries
nl_terse.description: A single sentence per tool naming its arguments inline. The cheapest prose variant, for the cost-normalised comparison.

nl_manpage.name: Unix man page style (novel)
nl_manpage.description: NAME / SYNOPSIS / DESCRIPTION / OPTIONS sections per tool. Prose and a formal synopsis line in one document — a genuinely hybrid presentation that no agent framework uses.

cli_help.name: Command-line --help output
cli_help.description: The output of `tool --help`: usage line, positional and optional arguments with inline help text. Extremely common in pretraining data and never used as a tool interface.

nl_faq.name: Question-and-answer tool guide (novel)
nl_faq.description: 'How do I check the weather? Call get_weather with city and optionally unit.' Presents tools as answers to user goals rather than as definitions — closer to how the model will be asked.

nl_narrative.name: Single flowing narrative (novel)
nl_narrative.description: The whole toolbox described in continuous prose with no list structure, no line breaks between tools, and no punctuation cues marking tool boundaries. The extreme end of the structure axis: all the information, none of the layout.

nl_instructional.name: Second-person instructions (novel)
nl_instructional.description: 'When the user asks about X, call get_weather and fill in city.' States tools as behavioural rules rather than as capabilities, which is how most production system prompts are actually written.

few_shot_only.name: Worked examples only, no schema (novel)
few_shot_only.description: Two filled-in example calls per tool and nothing else — no types, no descriptions, no required markers. Tests pure induction from instances, which is the cheapest possible interface that still names every argument.

nl_reference_card.name: Reference card (novel)
nl_reference_card.description: A compact reference card: tool name, a verb phrase, and its arguments as a bracketed slot list — `book_flight <from> <to> [class]`. Prose vocabulary with positional slots instead of keyword arguments.

python_stub.name: Python function stubs (Google docstrings)
python_stub.description: `def tool(arg: type = default) -> Return:` with a Google-style docstring. The single most familiar shape in pretraining data.

python_stub_numpy.name: Python function stubs (NumPy docstrings)
python_stub_numpy.description: Same stubs with NumPy-style section headers and underlines. Controls for docstring dialect inside the same language.

python_signature_only.name: Python signatures only
python_signature_only.description: One `def` line per tool, no docstring at all. The Python arm of the descriptions-off comparison, kept as its own format so the cheap variant is directly comparable.

python_pydantic.name: Pydantic models
python_pydantic.description: One `BaseModel` per tool with `Field(...)` descriptions and validation constraints. The shape most Python agent frameworks actually build schemas from.
python_pydantic.real_world_origin: Pydantic v2; LangChain / Instructor tool args

python_dataclass.name: Python dataclasses
python_dataclass.description: Argument bundles as `@dataclass` definitions plus a call function. Stdlib-only counterpart to the pydantic variant.

python_argparse.name: argparse parser construction (novel)
python_argparse.description: Each tool shown as the argparse code that would define its command line: add_argument calls carrying type, choices, default and help. A code-shaped way to state a schema that no agent framework uses today.

python_protocol.name: typing.Protocol tool interface
python_protocol.description: All tools as methods of one `class Tools(Protocol)`. Puts the whole universe in a single named scope instead of a flat list.

markdown_table.name: Markdown table
markdown_table.description: One pipe-delimited row per parameter, with the tool name repeated. Very dense; nesting is flattened into a bracketed type string.

csv.name: CSV table
csv.description: Comma-separated rows with a header line. No layout at all.

tsv.name: TSV table
tsv.description: Tab-separated variant of the CSV table: usually a few tokens cheaper.

ascii_table.name: Aligned ASCII table
ascii_table.description: Box-drawn, column-aligned table. Costs padding tokens but is the most visually parseable tabular variant.

key_value_lines.name: Key-value lines
key_value_lines.description: `tool.param: type (required) # doc`, one leaf per line. No delimiters, no nesting punctuation — the flattest readable form.

compact_signature_lines.name: Compact one-line signatures (novel)
compact_signature_lines.description: `tool_name: req_a:str req_b:int [opt_c:bool]` — one line per tool, square brackets for optional. Roughly the cheapest presentation that still names every argument and its type.

two_stage_index.name: Two-stage index then detail (novel)
two_stage_index.description: First a one-line index of every tool name and purpose, then the full schemas below. Gives the model a cheap routing pass before it has to read any schema — a direct test of whether tool-count decay is a search problem or a reading problem.

typescript.name: TypeScript function signatures
typescript.description: One `declare function` per tool with an inline parameter object, JSDoc comments for the prose, and named interfaces for nested objects.
typescript.real_world_origin: TypeScript; used by several agent frameworks

typescript_dts.name: TypeScript declaration file (.d.ts, namespaced)
typescript_dts.description: A `declare namespace tools { ... }` block: exactly the shape some vendors inject into system prompts for their built-in tools.

typescript_interface_arg.name: TypeScript single-argument interfaces
typescript_interface_arg.description: Every tool takes one typed args object declared as its own interface. Matches how JSON tool calls actually arrive, so the signature and the call shape line up exactly.

typescript_compact.name: TypeScript signatures, one line each
typescript_compact.description: Signature-only TypeScript: no comments, no interfaces, one line per tool. The cheapest presentation that still carries full types.

hermes_tools.name: Hermes <tools> block
hermes_tools.description: The NousResearch Hermes convention: JSON function signatures inside a <tools></tools> block, answered with <tool_call> tags. Adopted by a large number of open tool-use fine-tunes.

qwen_tools.name: Qwen tool template
qwen_tools.description: Qwen's chat template shape: a signature list inside <tools> with an explicit instruction to answer in <tool_call> JSON.

llama3_tools.name: Llama 3.x JSON tool listing
llama3_tools.description: The Llama 3.1+ prompt convention: 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke', followed by pretty-printed JSON and a strict response instruction.

mistral_tools.name: Mistral [AVAILABLE_TOOLS] block
mistral_tools.description: Mistral's control-token style listing: a JSON array wrapped in [AVAILABLE_TOOLS] ... [/AVAILABLE_TOOLS].

command_r_tools.name: Command-R Python-signature tool block
command_r_tools.description: Cohere Command-R's convention: tools shown as Python function definitions with typed docstrings, answered with a JSON list of tool_name / parameters objects.

react_tools.name: ReAct tool listing
react_tools.description: The classic ReAct/LangChain prompt: 'tool_name: description, args: {...}', answered with Thought/Action/Action Input. Predates native function calling and is still everywhere.

mcp_manifest.name: MCP tools/list response
mcp_manifest.description: The JSON-RPC result of an MCP `tools/list` call, verbatim. This is what a model sees when its tools come from MCP servers, which is now a very common deployment.

toolformer_inline.name: Toolformer inline API notation
toolformer_inline.description: The Toolformer convention: APIs described briefly and invoked inline in the text as [API(args)]. The call is part of the sentence rather than a separate message.

gorilla_api.name: Gorilla API-record listing
gorilla_api.description: The Gorilla / API-Bench record shape: domain, api_call template, api_arguments, functionality. An API-catalogue framing rather than a function-signature framing.

glaive_tools.name: Glaive SYSTEM function block
glaive_tools.description: The Glaive fine-tuning dataset convention: 'You are a helpful assistant with access to the following functions. Use them if required -' then bare JSON schemas.

xlam_tools.name: xLAM / APIGen tool block
xlam_tools.description: The xLAM (APIGen) convention: a JSON list of tools with typed parameter dicts, answered with a JSON list of {name, arguments} objects.

granite_tools.name: Granite <|tool|> block
granite_tools.description: IBM Granite's convention: a JSON array after a <|tool|> control marker, answered with <|tool_call|>.

dspy_signature.name: DSPy-style field signatures
dspy_signature.description: DSPy's declarative style: named InputField/OutputField declarations with descriptions, one signature class per tool.

openai_responses.name: OpenAI Responses API tool objects
openai_responses.description: The Responses API shape: flat objects with type/name/parameters and a strict flag. Structurally different from Chat Completions despite coming from the same vendor.

langchain_tools.name: LangChain render_text_description_and_args
langchain_tools.description: LangChain's default text rendering of a tool list: name, description and a JSON args schema on one line each.

watt_tool_tags.name: Compact tool-tag listing (watt-tool style)
watt_tool_tags.description: A very compact tag-delimited listing used by several small tool-tuned models: one line per tool inside a control block, no JSON at all.

yaml_schema.name: YAML schema (block style)
yaml_schema.description: The same JSON Schema content emitted as block-style YAML. The most common 'save tokens' recommendation in practice.
yaml_schema.real_world_origin: Widely used in agent prompt engineering

yaml_flow.name: YAML schema (flow style)
yaml_flow.description: YAML in flow style — inline maps and sequences on one line. Structurally identical to block YAML but visually JSON-like.

yaml_minimal.name: YAML (names and types only)
yaml_minimal.description: YAML counterpart of json_minimal: tool name, parameter names, types, required markers. Nothing else.

yaml_documented.name: YAML with comment documentation
yaml_documented.description: Structure in YAML, prose in `#` comments beside each key. Splits the documentation channel from the data channel.

yaml_anchors.name: YAML with anchors and aliases (novel)
yaml_anchors.description: Repeated sub-schemas are defined once under an anchor (&addr) and referenced with aliases (*addr). A large tool universe with shared structure shrinks a lot; the question is whether models can follow the indirection.

openapi_yaml.name: OpenAPI 3.1 (YAML)
openapi_yaml.description: Each tool as an OpenAPI operation with operationId, summary and a requestBody schema. What an agent sees when tools come from a real REST service.

openapi_json.name: OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON)
openapi_json.description: The same OpenAPI document serialised as JSON.
